title: Integration with kitty's icat for previewing images?
body:

- Shell
    - [x] bash
    - [ ] zsh

## Problem / Steps to reproduce

The kitty terminal emulator implements its own protocol for rendering graphics, called `icat`. It is possible to render images using the command `kitty +kitten icat $image.png`.

However, when running the follwing it does not work:

`fzf -q .png --preview="kitty +kitten icat {}"`

It results in the Preview pane just displaying "Loading.." .

Alongside the fact that neither iTerm's `imgcat` is supported (https://github.com/participant9/fzf/issues/1102) or the sixel format (https://github.com/participant9/fzf/issues/2544), there doesn't seem to be any way to preview images in fzf on MacOS, except the low fidelity (ASCII) `catimg`/`chafa`/etc.

It used to work with kitty's icat a while ago but it broke after the last update to the icat function. Its much faster now but now its unable to see that fzf is capable of supporting images. I've been looking for a solution for over a month now. Using an older version of Kitty and icat worked but its a hassle.

Currently Fzf mangles the escape codes for drawing sixel and icat has an issue with IO (I think it cant determine that the little fzf window is something supported by icat)

The only solution that I've been using in the intermediate is using Ueberzug since it uses X11 winodws as an overlay, or sending the command to a different Kitty window via fzf using the remote control functionality. I'd love to hear if anyone finds anything better or maybe knows a way to get it to work with Fzf. I tried to do it with version 0.1.0 and 0.7.1 hoping it would be easier to understand but I'm not skilled enough lol

Im on Linux with Zsh and bash. Idk if ueberzug works on Mac but its probably the best solution outside of adding image functionality to fzf.

Kitty plays videos and images really fast and with really high quality, Sixel is more widely supported but lower quality and easier to implement but they all basically do the same things.

comments.body:
With this commit, I can get icat working with fzf
https://github.com/participant8/kitty/commit/fc1331cfdc673c89eee711acd958ea09c0db8600

```sh
fzf -q .png --preview='kitten icat --clear --transfer-mode=memory --stdin=no --place=${FZF_PREVIEW_COLUMNS}x${FZF_PREVIEW_LINES}@participant15 {} > /dev/tty'
```

You of course need to adjust --place for your preview window though ideally FZF should set some env vars specifying the geometry of the preview window. Also there is a little display corruption, the cursor seems to end up on the wrong line in fzf, no idea whats going on with that, the icat kitten will leave the cursor at the top left of the image, maybe fzf is making some other assumptions about the cursor position. If so the command above could be modified to add some cursor movement escape codes after icat to position the cursor where fzf would like.

comments.author: participant9
comments.body:
Okay, the problem with the approach is that fzf runs the preview command in the background asynchronously and it is possible that kitty and fzf are both printing to `/dev/tty` at the same time causing unexpected rendering issues. So it looks like we do need a special mechanism from fzf's side anyway.

1. A special preview mode that redirects the output from the preview command to `/dev/tty`
    * `fzf --preview-raw 'kitty ... '`
    * `--preview-destination /dev/tty`
    * ...
    * This is the easiest option, but there will be few other use cases for it other than this
2. Make fzf understand kitty protocol and redirect the image part to `/dev/tty`
    * `\e_G` to `\e\\`
    * This would allow a preview command that prints both image and text. But it would be hard for fzf to properly support such commands because the preview window of fzf is scrollable.
3. Or ... ?

comments.author: participant8
comments.body:
If you want the most robust asynchronous preview option, I would suggest
the following:

1) Pass a temp dir to the preview script, possibly as an env var
2) If the preview script wants to output images it should write them as
PNG files in the that dir with names like 1.png, 2.png, ...
3) The preview script should output some simple escape code or
unicode placeholder char in its output text
4) When fzf sees that char/escape code it should read the next PNG image from the
dir and output it on the current line
5) Probably pass the preview window size in cells and pixels as env vars
so that the preview script can output correctly sized PNGs to avoid fzf
having to resize them.
6) When the preview area is cleared pass the escape code to clear any
images to the terminal.

This will require fzf to support basic image output but it preserves the
properties of asynchronicity and robustness.

Outputting a PNG image using the kitty protocol is dead simple, there
are 10 line bash and python scripts that do this here:
https://<redacted-host>/kitty/graphics-protocol/#a-minimal-example
Or you can just use the icat kitten to do it for you since it is no
longer asynchronous.

You will need to be a little more sophisticated to place the image in
the preview window area, but that will just be a couple of lines more of
code.

There are further complications that I suggest you dont need to worry
about for a MVP. Namely tmux, which if you want to support you will need
to use the unicode placeholders method of the kitty graphics protocol
(which icat supports) and also there are a few terminals that support only 
sixels but not kitty.

On Sun, Sep 24, 2023 at 11:00:38PM -0700, Junegunn Choi wrote:

comments.body:
Well the major downside of that is you lose both asynchronicity (you have to block fzf while the preview script is running) and you cant scroll the preview window any more. And it wont work inside tmux. 

Another option which gives you all of asynchronicity, scrolling and tmux support without fzf having to understand the kitty protocol is use

icat --unicode-placeholder

this will cause icat to output a bunch of PUA unicode characters in the image area (i.e. normal text) that will be replaced by the image. All fzf then needs to do is passthrough any graphics escape code to the tty which is easily done with a simple regex. Scrolling works just as with normal text since that is all there is.

Now fzf doesnt understand anything about the graphics protocol other than the start and end chars of the escape code. It just deals with plain text which it can scroll and have the image scroll normally. Even deleting the image is unnecessary as deleting the text will take care of it automatically.

comments.author: participant10
comments.body:
Glad to see some traction in this thread between the two creators :). And, finally a working solution, thanks to @participant8. 

Image preview now works with the latest kitty update (`0.30.1`). The following commands (modified from @participant8 command) can preview image and supports changes to window size but changing fzf's `preview-window` direction will need changes in icat's `--place` value. Although it isn't

Using fish:
```fish
EXTERNAL_COLUMNS=$COLUMNS \
fzf \
--preview='kitten icat --clear --transfer-mode=memory --place="$COLUMNS"x"$LINES"@(math $EXTERNAL_COLUMNS-$COLUMNS)x0 --align center --stdin=no {} > /dev/tty' \
--preview-window "right,50%,border-left"
```

Using bash:
```bash
EXTERNAL_COLUMNS=$COLUMNS \
fzf --preview='kitten icat --clear --transfer-mode=memory --place="$COLUMNS"x"$LINES"@"$(($EXTERNAL_COLUMNS-$COLUMNS))"x0 --align center --stdin=no {} > /dev/tty' \
--preview-window "right,50%,border-left"
```

zsh doesn't update `$COLUMNS` env var in fzf's preview window, so it requires some more hardcoding of `--place` values. A quick workaround is to use `$COLUMNS/2`.

> Also there is a little display corruption, the cursor seems to end up on the wrong line in fzf, no idea whats going on with that, the icat kitten will leave the cursor at the top left of the image, maybe fzf is making some other assumptions about the cursor position. If so the command above could be modified to add some cursor movement escape codes after icat to position the cursor where fzf would like.

Has anyone found a solution for this problem?

I have been playing around with it for a while and got pretty close to getting the image to display properly wherever the preview window is without breaking fzf's layout, but there is still an issue I can't solve.

```zsh
data=$(kitty icat \
    --clear \
    --transfer-mode=memory \
    --align center \
    --stdin=no \
    --unicode-placeholder \
    --place=${FZF_PREVIEW_COLUMNS}x${FZF_PREVIEW_LINES}@participant14 \
    {})
printf "$(sed "s/\x1b7.*$//" <<< $data)"
printf "\x1b7$(sed "s/^.*\x1b7//" <<< $data)" 1> /dev/tty
```

The idea is to use icat's `--unicode-placeholder` and print the placeholder characters (everything from `\x1b7`) to the preview window and the graphics data (everything before) directly to `/dev/tty`.

With this the image is well-aligned in the preview window and fzf doesn't get messed up. The only issue that's left now is that the area of the terminal where the image would appear normally (i.e. at `participant14`) is blacked out. We can slightly mitigate this by placing the image at `((${COLUMNS} - ${FZF_PREVIEW_COLUMNS}))x0` for a `position=right` preview window instead so that it often ends up unnoticeable but this is not a proper solution, just a bad hack.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
@participant11

Try something like this instead:
```sh
fd . ~/Pictures -e png | fzf --preview='kitty icat --clear --transfer-mode=memory --stdin=no --place=${FZF_PREVIEW_COLUMNS}x${FZF_PREVIEW_LINES}@participant14 {}'
```
`--align center` and `--place` are incompatible options if I remember correctly. The new PR that was merged detects the escape sequence for images and lets it pass through to the preview window unchanged. If you are dead set on using unicode placeholders for some reason then maybe check out `tupimage` but idk you would do that now. The workaround above is no longer required (displaying the image directly over /dev/tty) you can just update fzf to the newest version and use it directly.

comments.author: participant12
comments.body: Does anyone else have the issue where once displayed the kitty image preview doesn't disappear, both when a different non-image file is selected, or when fzf is exited? It looks like you can clear the image with `kitty icat --clear`, but I couldn't find a clean way to do this; trying to bind it to the `focus` event or even just adding `kitty icat --clear > /dev/null && bat -n --color=always {}` to the non-image part of the preview command appeared to cause strange behavior like non-image previews never loading. I'm using the [preview command suggested in the docs](https://github.com/participant9/fzf#previewing-an-image).

comments.author: participant11
comments.body:
> Try something like this instead:

Ah, thank you so much! I guess I must have never tried without deleting the last line with `sed` like the docs suggest; doing this leaves me with no image at all so I figured the solution doesn't work. Like this it's perfect!

---

> Does anyone else have the issue where once displayed the kitty image preview doesn't disappear, both when a different non-image file is selected, or when fzf is exited? It looks like you can clear the image with kitty icat --clear, but I couldn't find a clean way to do this; trying to bind it to the focus event or even just adding kitty icat --clear > /dev/null && bat -n --color=always {} to the non-image part of the preview command appeared to cause strange behavior like non-image previews never loading.

@participant12 I also had this issue but was able to fix it: I checked what `icat` prints to remove the image on `--clear`, which is `"\x1b_Ga=d,d=A\x1b\\"`. So if you just add the line

```sh
printf "\x1b_Ga=d,d=A\x1b\\"
```

to the unconditional section of your preview command instead of `kitty icat --clear` you will be good :)

(Note that you could also print this on the `focus` event like you suggested, but this makes the entire screen flash for me because it goes straight to your terminal, so it's better to do it on the `preview` command)
